# Welcome {.unnumbered}

The [ECS200 - Research Methods in Ecology](https://handbook.murdoch.edu.au/units/07/ecs200) 
workshops will go through the steps of a typical research project that looks 
something like **Figure 1**.

![**Fig. 1**. You start with data import and tidying. Next, you understand your data with an iterative cycle of transforming, visualizing, and modeling. You finish the process by communicating your results to other humans.](images/base.png)

First, you must **import** your data into R ([week 1](week1_getting_started.qmd)).
This usually means loading data stored in a file, database, or web application 
programming interface (API) into a data frame in R. If you can't get your data 
into R, you can't do any data science with it!

Once your data is imported, it’s a good idea to **tidy** it ([week 2](week2_tidy_data.qmd)).
Tidying means putting it into a consistent format where each column is a variable 
and each row is an observation. This alignment between the structure and meaning 
of the data makes analysis far easier. Tidy data lets you focus on answering 
questions rather than reformatting for each new task.

Next, you’ll often **transform** your data ([week 2](week2_tidy_data.qmd)).
This might include filtering for specific observations (e.g. animals from one 
site or data from the past year), creating new variables (e.g. calculating speed
from distance and time), or summarising patterns (e.g. counts or averages). Tidying 
and transforming are often called wrangling, because getting data into a usable 
form can feel like a struggle!

Once you have tidy, relevant data, you’ll typically turn to two main tools:
visualisation and modelling. These are complementary, and most analyses move 
back and forth between them.

- **Visualisation** is fundamental ([week 4](week4_descriptive_stats.qmd)).
A good plot can reveal unexpected patterns or raise new questions.
It might even suggest you’re asking the wrong question or need better data.
Visualisations can be powerful—but they don’t scale well, since they rely on 
human interpretation.

- **Models** (week 5 to week 13) complement visualisation. Once you’ve clearly 
defined your questions, a model can help answer them. Models are mathematical 
or computational, so they scale well—and if needed, more computers are easier 
to get than more people! However, models come with assumptions and can't question 
those assumptions or truly surprise you.

The final step in data science is **communication** (visualisation and model weeks).
Even the best models or visuals are useless unless you can clearly explain your
findings to others. Effective communication is critical.

Surrounding all these activities is **programming**. You’ll use code throughout
every step of a data science project. You don’t need to be a programming expert,
but improving your coding skills pays off—it helps you automate tasks and solve 
problems more efficiently.


## Unit Learning Objectives

At the end of the unit, students should be able to:

1. **Design** ecological research using appropriate sampling strategies and 
analytical methods.
2. Apply appropriate **statistical methods** to test ecological hypotheses.
3. Apply **R programming** to process, analyse, and visualise ecological datasets 
to professional standards.
4. Critically **evaluate** the strengths and limitations of research designs 
under different ecological conditions.
5. **Communicate** the findings of ecological research to professional standards.
